content: Allopurinol is a medication prescribed to treat gout, elevated levels of uric acid in the body caused by certain cancer treatments, and kidney stones. It belongs to a class of drugs known as xanthine oxidase inhibitors. This medication works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid can lead to gout attacks or kidney stones. It is important to note that allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol is available in tablet form and is taken orally, usually once or twice daily, preferably after a meal. To ensure consistent use, it is recommended to take it at the same time every day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take allopurinol exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it or take it more frequently than prescribed. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and gradually increase it, typically no more than once a week. It may take several months or longer to experience the full benefits of allopurinol. During the initial months of treatment, you may experience an increase in gout attacks, but the medication will eventually help prevent them. Your doctor may prescribe another medication, such as colchicine, to prevent gout attacks during the first few months of allopurinol use. Continue taking allopurinol even if you feel well, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Allopurinol is sometimes used to treat seizures, pain caused by pancreatic disease, and certain infections. It may also be used to improve survival after bypass surgery, reduce ulcer relapses, and prevent rejection of kidney transplants. Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Allopurinol may also be prescribed for other uses; ask your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking allopurinol, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to allopurinol or any other medications. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention medications such as amoxicillin, ampicillin, anticoagulants like warfarin, cancer chemotherapy drugs like cyclophosphamide and mercaptopurine, chlorpropamide, diuretics, immunosuppressants like azathioprine and cyclosporine, other gout medications like probenecid and sulfinpyrazone, and tolbutamide. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have or have ever had kidney or liver disease or heart failure. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking allopurinol, contact your doctor immediately. Be aware that allopurinol may cause drowsiness. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you. Consult your doctor about the safe use of alcoholic beverages while taking allopurinol, as alcohol may reduce its effectiveness. While taking allopurinol, drink at least eight glasses of water or other fluids daily unless otherwise directed by your doctor. If you miss a dose of allopurinol, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Allopurinol may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms and they are severe or persistent: upset stomach, diarrhea, or drowsiness. Some side effects can be serious. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience any of the following: skin rash, painful urination, blood in the urine, eye irritation, swelling of the lips or mouth, fever, sore throat, chills, signs of infection, loss of appetite, unexpected weight loss, or itching. If you experience any unusual problems while taking this medication, contact your doctor. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store allopurinol in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of outdated or no longer needed medication properly. Consult your pharmacist about the appropriate disposal method. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor will order specific lab tests to monitor your body’s response to allopurinol. Do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, ask your pharmacist.
